title: Sharif Says Pakistan Can Reach Sixth-Largest Economy Before 2050, Not 2075
excerpt: Addressing a minerals investment forum in Islamabad, Pakistan's prime minister amended a Goldman Sachs projection that places his country sixth in the world by 2075, saying the milestone can arrive more than 25 years earlier.
body:
• Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif told the Pakistan Minerals Investment Forum 2026 in Islamabad on Friday, November 13, 2026, that Pakistan can become the world's sixth-largest economy earlier than 2050.
  • That is Sharif's own amendment, not a Goldman Sachs forecast: the bank's assessment he cited projects Pakistan sixth by 2075, more than 25 years later.
  • The Goldman Sachs study, published in December 2022, conditions that 2075 ranking on appropriate policies and institutions, and does not place Pakistan in its top five for 2050.
  • Sharif tied the ambition to minerals, urging investors to process and manufacture in Pakistan instead of exporting raw minerals, and pointed to the Reko Diq copper and gold project, with production expected to begin in 2028.

Pakistan's prime minister has publicly moved up his country's economic deadline by more than a quarter of a century. Addressing the concluding session of the Pakistan Minerals Investment Forum 2026 in Islamabad on Friday, Shehbaz Sharif cited a Goldman Sachs assessment that projects Pakistan as the world's sixth-largest economy by 2075, and then revised the date himself, according to The News and the Pakistan Observer.

"I would like to make a small amendment here — instead of 2075, it will be earlier than 2050."

— Shehbaz Sharif, Prime Minister of Pakistan

What Goldman Sachs Actually Projected

The assessment Sharif cited is "The Path to 2075," a December 2022 paper by Goldman Sachs economists Kevin Daly and Tadas Gedminas. As Clash Report notes in its account of the speech, the study projects Pakistan as the sixth-largest economy in 2075, measured in real U.S. dollars, behind China, India, the United States, Indonesia and Nigeria, in that order. Accounts of the paper put Pakistan's projected real GDP at $12.7 trillion in 2075, with GDP per capita of $27,100.

The same paper is more cautious than the headline suggests. Its authors describe the results less as a forecast and more as a way of uncovering broad global dynamics, and they condition Pakistan's rise on the country having the appropriate policies and institutions, with population growth as the main driver. For 2050, the midpoint Sharif is now targeting, the paper's five largest economies are China, the United States, India, Indonesia and Germany. Pakistan does not appear in that top five.

A Minerals Pitch Behind the Claim

Sharif made the remarks while asking foreign investors to build Pakistan's mining sector. He said the country aims to stop exporting its valuable mineral resources in raw form and instead use them in domestic industries, and he pointed to the establishment of a National Minerals Data Centre and the digitisation of geological records. Referring to Reko Diq, he described it as one of the world's largest undeveloped copper and gold deposits, said the project had remained stalled for two decades, and said it is now moving towards its operational phase. Other reporting from the forum put the expected start of Reko Diq production in 2028.

Speaking at the same session, Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir said Pakistan aims to become a competitive destination for long-term mineral investment and that measures are being taken to ensure the security of the mining ecosystem, according to The News.

The Starting Point

The distance to sixth place is considerable. The International Monetary Fund estimates Pakistan's 2026 nominal GDP at about $450 billion, ranking the country 42nd in the world, and Pakistan remains in a $7 billion Extended Fund Facility with the Fund. IMF staff reached agreement in October on the programme's fourth review, which would release about $1 billion if the IMF board approves it.

Sharif acknowledged the difficulty in his own remarks, saying the journey of development would have to continue despite economic difficulties and long challenges, and that efforts should not be abandoned. The Pakistan Observer reported that he stressed sustained high growth, exports, industrial development, investment, productivity and economic stability would be fundamental to reaching the goal.

What to Watch

No new Goldman Sachs projection supports the earlier date; the before-2050 timeline is a government ambition stated by the prime minister, not a revised bank forecast. Whether it gains credibility will depend on measurable steps investors can track: Reko Diq's progress towards its expected 2028 production start, continued IMF programme reviews, and whether mineral agreements signed around the forum convert into processing and manufacturing plants inside Pakistan rather than raw exports.
